'''Rudolph Arthur Marcus''' (July 21, 1923 – July 16, 2026) was a Canadian-born American chemist who received the 1992 [[Nobel Prize in Chemistry]] "for his contributions to the theory of [[electron transfer]] reactions in chemical systems".<ref name="nobel">{{cite web|url=https://www.nobelprize.org/nobel_prizes/chemistry/laureates/1992/ |title=The Nobel Prize in Chemistry 1992 |publisher=Nobelprize.org |access-date=2013-08-01|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131005043823/http://www.nobelprize.org/nobel_prizes/chemistry/laureates/1992/index.html|archive-date=October 5, 2013|url-status=dead}}</ref> [[Marcus theory]], named after him, provides a [[Thermodynamics|thermodynamic]] and [[Kinetics (chemistry)|kinetic]] framework for describing one electron [[outer-sphere electron transfer]].<ref>[http://nobelprize.org/chemistry/laureates/1992/marcus-autobio.html Rudolph A. Marcus: autobiography]</ref><ref>[http://nobelprize.org/chemistry/laureates/1992/marcus-lecture.html Rudolph A. Marcus: Nobel Lecture 1992, Electron Transfer Reactions in Chemistry: Theory and Experiment]</ref><ref>[http://www.vega.org.uk/video/programme/39 Freeview video 'An Interview with Rudolph Marcus' by the Vega Science Trust]</ref> He was a professor at [[California Institute of Technology|Caltech]], [[Nanyang Technological University]], [[Singapore]] and a member of the [[International Academy of Quantum Molecular Science]].
== Education and early life ==
Rudolph Arthur Marcus was born in [[Montreal]], Quebec, on July 21, 1923, the son of Esther (born Cohen) and Myer Marcus. His father was born in New York and his mother was born in England. His family originated in [[Ukmergė]], Lithuania, then part of [[Russian Empire|Russia]].<ref name=":0">Marcus, Rudolph A. Interview by Shirley K. Cohen. Pasadena, California, December 1, 7, and 14, 1993. Oral History Project, California Institute of Technology Archives. Retrieved 2020 from the World Wide Web: https://digital.archives.caltech.edu/collections/OralHistories/OH_Marcus_R/OH_Marcus_R.pdf</ref> He was [[Jews|Jewish]]<ref>{{Cite web|title=Jewish Nobel Prize Laureates|url=https://www.jewishvirtuallibrary.org/jewish-nobel-prize-laureates|access-date=2020-11-06|website=Jewish Virtual Library}}</ref> and grew up mostly in a Jewish neighbourhood in Montreal but also spent some of his childhood in [[Detroit]], United States.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Rudolph A. Marcus |url=https://oh.sciencehistory.org/oral-histories/marcus-rudolph-a|access-date=2020-11-06|website=Center for Oral History}}</ref><ref name=":0" /> His interest in the sciences began at a young age. He excelled at mathematics at [[Baron Byng High School]]. He then studied at [[McGill University]] under [[Carl A. Winkler]],<ref name=TranscriptCHF>{{cite book|first= James J. |last=Bohning|title=Rudolph A. Marcus, Transcript of an Interview Conducted by James J. Bohning in Pasadena, California on 20 June 1991 |date=20 June 1991 |url=https://oh.sciencehistory.org/sites/default/files/marcus_ra_0097_suppl.pdf|place=Philadelphia, PA|publisher=[[Chemical Heritage Foundation]] }}</ref> who had studied under [[Cyril Hinshelwood]] at the [[University of Oxford]]. At McGill, Marcus took more math courses than an average chemistry student, which would later aid him in creating his theory on electron transfer.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nobelprize.org/nobel_prizes/chemistry/laureates/1992/marcus.html |title=Rudolph A. Marcus – Facts |publisher=Nobelprize.org |date=1923-07-21 |access-date=2013-08-01}}</ref>

Marcus earned a [[Bachelor of Science|B.Sc.]] in 1943 and a [[Doctor of Philosophy|Ph.D.]] in 1946, both from McGill University.<ref name=OralHistoryCHF>{{cite web|author=Center for Oral History| title= Rudolph A. Marcus |url=https://oh.sciencehistory.org/oral-histories/marcus-rudolph-a|website= [[Science History Institute]] }}</ref><ref name="thesis-marcus-1946">{{cite thesis |url=https://central.bac-lac.gc.ca/.item?id=TC-QMM-125985&op=pdf&app=Library |title=Studies on the conversion of PHX to AcAn |date=1946 |publisher=[[McGill University]] |degree=Ph.D. |last=Marcus |first=Rudolph A. |oclc=903054593}}</ref> In 1958, he became a [[naturalized citizen]] of the United States.

== Career and research ==
After graduating, in 1946, he took postdoctoral positions first at the [[National Research Council (Canada)]],<ref>{{cite web|url=https://oh.sciencehistory.org/sites/default/files/marcus_ra_0097_suppl.pdf|title=Oral history interview with Rudolph A. Marcus}}</ref> followed by the [[University of North Carolina]]. He received his first faculty appointment at the [[Polytechnic Institute of Brooklyn]]. In 1952, at the University of North Carolina, he developed [[RRKM theory|Rice–Ramsperger–Kassel–Marcus]] (RRKM) theory by combining the former RRK theory with the [[transition state theory]]. In 1964, he taught at the [[University of Illinois]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.britannica.com/EBchecked/topic/364323/Rudolph-A-Marcus |title=Rudolph A. Marcus (Canadian-American chemist) |publisher=Britannica|date=1923-07-21 |access-date=2013-08-01}}</ref> Marcus moved to the [[California Institute of Technology]] in 1978.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://digital.sciencehistory.org/works/fl0l2nf |title=Oral history interview with Rudolph A. Marcus |work=[[Science History Institute]]}}</ref> His approach to solving a problem was to "go full tilt"{{Spaced en dash}}he said echoing his interviewer in ''Veery Journal''{{Spaced en dash}}pursuing the problem until he either reached an answer or decided it was time to put the problem aside for a while.<ref>{{Cite interview|last=Marcus|first=Rudolph A.|interviewer-last=Vita|interviewer-first=Steven | date=1996|title=Nobel Laureate Scientist Rudolph A. Marcus|url=http://veeryjournal.com/nobel-laureate-rudolph-a-marcus-interview.html|access-date=2021-04-20|website=Veery Journal|language=en}}</ref>

=== Marcus theory of electron transfer ===
[[Electron transfer]] is one of the simplest forms of a chemical reaction. It consists of one [[Outer sphere electron transfer|outer-sphere electron transfer]] between substances of the same atomic structure likewise to Marcus's studies between divalent and trivalent iron ions. Electron transfer may be one of the most basic forms of chemical reaction but without it life cannot exist. Electron transfer is used in all [[Respiratory system|respiratory]] functions as well as [[photosynthesis]]. In the process of [[Redox|oxidizing]] food molecules, two hydrogen ions, two electrons, and half an oxygen molecule react to make an [[exothermic reaction]] as well as a water molecule:

: 2 H<sup>+</sup> + 2 e<sup>−</sup> + ½ O<sub>2</sub> → H<sub>2</sub>O + heat{{Citation needed|date=August 2024}}

Because electron transfer is such a broad, common, and essential reaction within nature, Marcus's theory has become vital within the field of chemistry and [[biochemistry]].

A type of chemical reaction linked to his many studies of electron transfer would be the transfer of an electron between metal ions in different states of oxidation. An example of this type of chemical reaction would be one between a divalent and a trivalent iron ion in an aqueous solution. In Marcus's time chemists were astonished at the slow rate in which this specific reaction took place. This attracted many chemists in the 1950s and is also what began Marcus's interests in electron transfer. Marcus made many studies based on the principles that were found within this chemical reaction, and through his studies was able to elaborate his electron transfer theory. His approach gave way to new experimental programs that contributed to all branches within chemistry and biochemistry.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.cce.caltech.edu/faculty/marcus/index.html |title=Faculty – Division of Chemistry and Chemical Engineering – Caltech |publisher=Cce.caltech.edu |access-date=2013-08-01 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130806195818/http://www.cce.caltech.edu/faculty/marcus/index.html |archive-date=2013-08-06 }}</ref>

== Later life and death ==
As of his 100th birthday, he was still actively conducting research.<ref name=illinois /><ref>{{Cite Q|Q141147852}}</ref> He died at his home in [[Pasadena, California]], on July 16, 2026, five days shy of his 103rd birthday.<ref name="NYTobit">{{cite news |last1=McClain |first1=Dylan Loeb |title=Rudolph Marcus, Who Illuminated Electrochemical Processes, Dies at 102 |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2026/07/17/science/rudolph-marcus-dead.html |access-date=17 July 2026 |publisher=The New York Times |date=17 July 2026}}</ref>

Marcus also received a professorial fellowship at [[University College, Oxford]], from 1975 to 1976.

Marcus was elected to the [[National Academy of Sciences]] in 1970, the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]] in 1973, the [[American Philosophical Society]] in 1990, received honorary membership in the [[Royal Society of Chemistry]] in 1991, and in the [[Royal Society of Canada]] in 1993.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nobelprize.org/nobel_prizes/chemistry/laureates/1992/marcus-autobio.html |title=Rudolph A. Marcus – Biographical |publisher=Nobelprize.org |access-date=2013-08-01}}</ref> He was elected a [[List of Fellows of the Royal Society elected in 1987|Foreign Member of the Royal Society (ForMemRS) in 1987]].<ref name=formemrs>{{cite web|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151010213527/https://royalsociety.org/people/rudolph-marcus-11894/|archive-date=2015-10-10|url=https://royalsociety.org/people/rudolph-marcus-11894/|title=Professor Rudolph Marcus ForMemRS|publisher=[[Royal Society]]|location=London}}</ref>

In 2019, Marcus was awarded the Fray International Sustainability award at SIPS 2019 by FLOGEN Star Outreach.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.flogen.org/?p=38&bio=Marcus|title=Rudy Marcus Winner of the Fray Award}}</ref>
